extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, researchers and clinicians interested in peer review practice and policy (medical/biomedical readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary and evaluative guidance on peer review models, their advantages/disadvantages, controversies and good-practice measures for conducting and overseeing peer review in medical/biomedical journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers aim to provide a critical, independent and unbiased assessment of submitted manuscripts to identify weaknesses and improve work prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the role of peer review as an extension of the scientific process, increasing probability that mistakes or flaws will be detected; helps editors decide suitability for publication and functions as gatekeeping for the body of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer qualifications and suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewing requires a community of experts in a defined field who are qualified, willing and able to perform impartial reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should select reviewers with appropriate expertise and willingness; suitability includes domain expertise, impartiality and ability to provide independent critical assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-blinded peer review (variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-blinded review: reviewers know authors' identities while authors do not know reviewers'. One subtype is 'author-guided review' where authors can suggest or exclude reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages of author-guided: authors can exclude biased reviewers and suggest appropriate expertise; easier for editors to find specialised reviewers and possibly faster. Disadvantages/anti-patterns: potential reviewer fraud, distortion of scientific process and risk of bias from reviewers who know authors (harsh on rivals or deference to 'big name' authors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blinded peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blinded review: neither authors nor reviewers know each other's identities; currently used by many medical journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include reduction of reviewer bias (protecting early-career, women, minorities, and lesser-known institutions). Limitations: difficult to fully blind in small fields, time-consuming for editorial office to anonymise manuscripts, and does not eliminate potential for reviewer misconduct (e.g., plagiarism of ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple-blinded peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Triple-blinded review: handling editor, reviewer and author are all anonymous to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to further reduce bias; similar practical and ethical concerns as double-blind, and risk that anonymity can still permit reviewer misconduct such as plagiarising unpublished ideas or data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent peer review (reports published, reviewers unnamed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer reports are published with the article but reviewers are not named, increasing transparency about the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes editorial correspondence is also published to show basis for editorial decisions; intended to allow readers to assess review quality without revealing reviewer identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review (named reviewers, pre- and post-publication variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review: authors and reviewers are known to each other; can be pre-publication (reports and reviewer names published alongside article versions) or post-publication (ongoing public commentary after publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: speed, transparency, accountability, recognition for reviewers, educative value for early-career researchers, easier detection of conflicts of interest. Disadvantages: reviewers may be reluctant to be critical, may give unjustified praise to avoid offending powerful authors, difficulty recruiting reviewers, and potential reduction in candour. Reviewers may nonetheless be allowed confidential comments to editors in some models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid systems combine elements of open and blinded review (e.g., blinded review followed by publication of open reviews), or run open reviews in parallel with closed reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid can offer benefits of both systems (transparency plus anonymous initial assessment) but at cost of increased time and expense. Modified hybrids include post-acceptance open review similar to some journal experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint/decoupled/sequential review
rubrics_metrics.description: Variants where manuscripts are uploaded to preprint servers enabling open community comments, decoupled review by other organizations, or sequential review starting from preprint and followed by formal commissioned review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can enable broad community participation and iterative improvement. Risks include difficulty ensuring rigorous pre-publication review and potential undermining of trust if inadequate review is combined with rapid dissemination of medical results (medical organisations have warned about inadequate pre-publication review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ongoing review after publication via letters to the editor, online comment forums, blogs, social media (e.g., Facebook), independent sites like PubPeer, and services that aggregate post-publication ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables readers to continue scrutiny, has helped uncover fraud leading to retractions; formats vary in moderation, anonymity options, and potential for whistle-blowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient peer review and patient involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruiting patients, patient advocates and carers as reviewers to give feedback alongside academic reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation points include whether study issues are relevant to patients, whether patient challenges are highlighted, and whether the intervention has potential patient benefits. Advantages: inclusion and empowerment, co-produced publication models, new reviewer talent pool. Concerns: tokenism, failure to systematically use patient data, inability to capture authentic patient voice, transparency and commercial influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of peer review to detect errors and fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is generally poor at detecting gross defects and is not designed primarily to detect fraud; reviewers often miss methodological errors or unsupported conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reviewers should request additional information when warranted (including raw data), consider audits of reviewer reports for quality control, and recognise limitations of peer review in detecting clever fraud (which may be found later by replication or data access).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards against manipulated or fraudulent peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures to prevent fake or manipulated reviews (e.g., fabricated reviewer accounts, falsified email addresses used in author-suggested reviewer schemes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers/journals should consider ending or tightly controlling author-suggested reviewers, use secure reviewer account verification, follow COPE guidance on inappropriate manipulation, and investigate suspicious reviewer behaviour; past incidents led some publishers to discontinue author nominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks from predatory journals and inadequate peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory journals often charge fees but provide negligible or no peer review and fail to meet scholarly standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and readers should be wary of negligible peer review; lack of constructive review harms authors and misleads readers. Journals and institutions should promote publication venues with credible peer review practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and linguistic bias (anglocentrism) in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: A predominance of native English-speaking editors and reviewers can lead to bias against manuscripts that do not match preferred 'good scientific English style'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit a more diverse reviewer pool reflective of cultural and linguistic diversity and varied healthcare/research experiences to reduce unfair judgements about writing and increase equity for non-Anglophone authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired reviewer attributes and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers should be well-trained, open-minded and diligent, providing evaluations performed to the best of their knowledge and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training and guidance for reviewers improve review quality. Journals should consider mechanisms to recognise, retain and reward good reviewers and provide educational value to early-career reviewers by making reviews visible (where appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and quality assurance of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must have oversight of and ensure the robustness and quality assurance of their journal’s peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures include editors requesting additional information (raw data) when necessary, auditing reviewer reports for quality control, selecting appropriate review models for the journal community, and ensuring processes reduce bias and misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics and evaluative criteria for peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Ways to assess peer review models include speed, transparency, accountability, likelihood of attracting reviewers, cost/time to complete reviews, propensity to reduce bias, and effect on publication outcomes (e.g., representation of female authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys and studies (e.g., Publons, Nature-branded journal analyses, F1000Prime) provide empirical evidence of authors' and reviewers' preferences and model effects (e.g., preference for blinded review, double-blind increasing female first-authored papers). Use multiple metrics when choosing or evaluating a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication rating systems (example: F1000Prime features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication services can provide structured ratings and metadata: F1000Prime uses star ratings, tags (e.g., 'controversial', 'changes clinical practice'), a brief review, reasons for recommendation and potential implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features serve as a form of ongoing peer evaluation and article discovery; they aggregate individual reviewer scores to rank articles and summarise expert opinion for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs between openness and reviewer recruitment/candour
rubrics_metrics.description: Open review improves transparency and recognition but may reduce reviewer willingness to participate and decrease critical candour due to fear of professional repercussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal policy should balance transparency with practical ability to recruit quality reviewers; hybrid or optional signing may be used to mitigate trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition, retention and rewarding of peer reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because peer reviewers are a valuable resource, journals should find innovative ways to recognise, retain and reward good peer reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include formal recognition, credit systems, visibility of high-quality reviews, and incentives to sustain reviewer engagement and quality.
